items.heading: Fixing a leaking or dripping tap
precautionsFirst: Turn off the isolation valve for that tap before starting.
Keep a cloth or bucket handy to catch residual water.
Note the order of parts as you disassemble the tap so reassembly is easy.
details: Shut off the isolation valve under the sink, or the main supply if there is none.
Unscrew the tap handle and the retaining nut to reach the spindle.
Pull out the spindle and inspect the rubber washer at the end for wear or cracks.
Replace the washer with a new one of the same size.
Reassemble the tap, turn the water supply back on, and check for leaks.

items.heading: Unclogging a slow or blocked sink drain
precautionsFirst: Avoid mixing chemical drain cleaners with other cleaning products, which can produce harmful fumes.
Wear rubber gloves when clearing debris by hand.
details: Remove any visible debris from the drain opening by hand or with a wire hook.
Pour half a cup of baking soda followed by half a cup of vinegar down the drain, and let it fizz for 10-15 minutes.
Flush with a kettle of hot, not boiling, water for plastic pipes.
If still blocked, use a plunger with a firm up-and-down motion to dislodge the clog.
For a persistent clog, open the U-shaped trap pipe under the sink over a bucket and clear it by hand.

items.heading: Unclogging a blocked toilet
precautionsFirst: Wear gloves and make sure the bathroom is well ventilated.
Do not use a plunger right after adding chemical cleaners, as splashing can occur.
details: Use a toilet plunger, ensuring it fully covers the drain hole, and pump firmly several times.
If unsuccessful, feed a toilet auger (snake) gently into the drain to break up the blockage.
Pour a bucket of water from waist height into the bowl in one go - this can help dislodge a partial clog.
If it stays blocked or overflow risk is high, call a plumber rather than continuing to force it.

items.heading: Fixing a running toilet cistern
precautionsFirst: Turn off the water supply valve behind the toilet before working inside the cistern for long.
details: Remove the cistern lid and watch the flush mechanism while it fills.
Check the float ball or cup moves freely and shuts the inlet valve once the tank is full.
Lower the float arm or float height slightly if the water level is too high and overflowing into the overflow tube.
Check the flapper or flush valve seal at the bottom is not warped or leaking into the bowl, and replace it if worn.

items.heading: Low water pressure from a tap or showerhead
precautionsFirst: Turn off the water supply before removing any fitting.
details: Unscrew the aerator or showerhead nozzle by hand, or with pliers wrapped in cloth to avoid scratching.
Soak the aerator or nozzle in a bowl of vinegar for 30-60 minutes to dissolve mineral deposits.
Scrub gently with an old toothbrush and rinse thoroughly.
Reattach and check if flow improves - if not, the issue may be in the supply line and needs a plumber.

items.heading: Temporary fix for a leaking pipe joint
precautionsFirst: This is a temporary measure only - have the pipe properly repaired or replaced by a plumber soon after.
Turn off the main water supply before attempting any fix.
details: Shut off the water supply to the affected pipe.
Dry the pipe surface thoroughly around the leak.
Wrap self-fusing silicone tape, or plumber's epoxy putty, tightly around the leaking joint, overlapping each layer.
Turn the water supply back on slowly and check for continued leaking.
Arrange a permanent repair with a plumber as soon as possible.

items.heading: Air lock causing sputtering or no flow from a tap
precautionsFirst: Do not connect hot and cold supply hoses together, as pressure differences can cause issues.
details: Attach a hose between a working tap with good pressure and the affected tap, both fully open.
Let water run through for a minute or two to push the trapped air out, or open and close the affected tap rapidly a few times.
Turn off both taps and test the affected tap on its own.
